About

Gilda Manfrin is a Milan-based creative working across content direction, strategy and visual communication.

Her practice brings together commissioned projects, editorial research and teaching at NABA and IED, where she works with fashion communication, digital strategy and visual methods.

Alongside her visual work, she composes and records music for piano and electronics.

A FEW QUESTIONS — MAKING PLANETS / 04 / 2026
A Few Questions 04 / ELECTROCUTE LAB

On building worlds of your own

Making Planets is a series of short exchanges on independent creative practices and the ways distinctive creative worlds are built, sustained and allowed to evolve.

ELECTROCUTE LAB is a creative practice bringing together electronics, textiles, poetry, and craft, exploring technology in a tactile, personal and handmade way.

01Origins

First of all, I have to say I love the name Electrocute Lab! I actually wanted to start an electropop band called Electrocutes back in my university days :-) Your practice brings together electronics, textiles, poetry, and craft. How did these seemingly different interests come together, and what first drew you to exploring technology in such a tactile and personal way?

Thank you! Electrocutes would have been such a great band name! I actually hear that often from people. Electrocute has been with me since around 2015, maybe even earlier. It's kind of my alter ego. In person I'm quiet and calm, sometimes shy, and Electrocute is the brighter side of me, everything glowing underneath. At some point I realized it could be my online alias too. I wish it could have just been Electrocute, but the username wasn't available, so I added "Lab" to it, and it's stayed that way ever since. I think the name is often what brings people in on social media, and because it doesn't belong to any one field, the people who find me come from all kinds of areas: electronics, music, craft, art, design. I really love that, because Electrocute Lab is a mix of all of those things, and it's meant to be for everyone.

As for how it all came together, I was a STEAM kid before the term was really a thing. Art and science never felt separate to me. It started with the family computer, which technically belonged to everyone but was really mine. I was the kid who fixed whatever broke and taught herself HTML making Neopets pages and MySpace layouts. I grew up during the Y2K era, so I've seen firsthand how much technology has changed from then until now. It's interesting that there's such a trendy nostalgia for that time right now, but I have to say, it truly was the best era! Computers were the first thing I loved figuring out, and I never stopped tinkering. I've also been a writer my whole life, and after a few detours I studied computer science, which brought the two together.

Textiles came later, when I got curious about the long history connecting weaving and computation. That's when I started thinking of a computer as something you could make by hand, not just buy. I've always paid close attention to materials and how things feel in your hands, and when you build something yourself, you understand every part of it. It stops feeling like a sealed box someone else made. That closeness is what I keep coming back to.

02The Soft Computer

Could you tell us a little more about The Soft Computer? How does it actually work, in simple terms, and what inspired you to create it? Was there a particular need or question that sparked the project?

The Soft Computer was my master's thesis at New York University's (NYU) Interactive Telecommunications Program (ITP), part of the Tisch School of the Arts. It's a textile computing object. There are still embedded electronics powering the interaction, but they live beneath a larger soft shell. Its machine-knit body holds a flexible e-ink display and two small computers, a Raspberry Pi and an Adafruit Fruit Jam. They talk to each other, and each one handles different parts of the experience.

On the front are four felt buttons, each a different color. They're made with conductive fabric and tape, so when you press one, the two conductive layers touch and close a small circuit, which the computer reads as a press. Each button is tied to its own collection of text: one about care, one that's dreamlike, one about textiles, and one made from computer science documentation that I've bent a little. When you press a button, the computer recombines fragments from that collection into something new. I wouldn't say it writes. It shuffles language that already exists and hands a piece of it back to you, showing it on the screen and printing it on a small thermal printer as a keepsake you can take with you.

The question behind it was simple: what would a computer feel like if it were soft, slow, and asked nothing of you? Most of our devices are hard, fast, and built to hold our attention. I wanted to make one that does the opposite, and I made it fully open source so other people can build their own.

03Computing as a craft

You describe your approach as "computing as a craft", which I find particularly clever. How did this vision emerge, and how does it change the way you think about designing and making technology?

It came from noticing that I approach code and circuits the same way I approach arts and crafts: slowly, by hand, and paying attention to materials. The more I learned about the history of computing, the more natural that felt. Computation has a long relationship with textiles. The Jacquard loom used punch cards to weave patterns in the early 1800s, and that same idea later found its way into early computers. The first programmers of ENIAC were women who programmed it by hand, plugging in cables and setting switches. And the memory for the Apollo missions was core rope memory, woven by hand, mostly by women, threading wire through tiny magnetic cores. Computing has always had craft in it. Somewhere along the way it just got hidden inside sealed, glossy boxes.

That's really what handmade computing means to me: bringing that part back into view. Craft means caring about how something is made and not only whether it works. When I think of computing that way, I start from different questions. How does this feel to hold? What is it made of? Can someone open it up and repair it? Does it really need to be fast, or connected, or smart? Sometimes the answer is no, and that frees me to make something quieter.

It also changes how I build. I often leave circuits visible instead of hiding them, I use soft materials like felt and conductive fabric where you'd normally find plastic, and I design things to be repaired and passed along. And it keeps the work small on purpose. I'd rather make one object carefully, or a few in a small batch, than something built to scale.

04Poetronics

Your practice spans different areas of experimentation, including Poetronics and Craft Computery. Could you tell us a little more about what these projects actually involve, how you work across them, and what directions you're most curious to explore further?

Poetronics is the framework for all of it. I describe it as electronics shaped by the sensibility of a poem, made to slow you down. In practice that means small devices that work with language and time, like a clock that shows you poetic messages and only reveals the actual time now and then, or a one-button object that generates poems.

Craft Computery is actually a new name. It started out as Soft Interfaces, but I realized I don't only make soft interfaces, I make all kinds of other things too. So I wanted a name that could hold everything, and I liked the idea of something like a brewery, but for computing and craft. It's now the craft-tech R&D division of Electrocute Lab, where I share how things are made: soft interfaces, tiny computing, and what I call gentle engineering. It's also a tiny shop (launching soon). What makes it a little different is that it shows the process first, a glimpse of how each thing is made, and then the finished piece. It'll carry both digital and physical things, all handmade and released slowly in small batches.

Looking ahead, I'm most curious about turning the Soft Computer's interface into its own small operating system for e-ink screens, and about going even smaller with tiny displays and tiny computers.

05Uncertainty

We are living through a time of great uncertainty. Does this affect the way you think about your work and its future? What helps you keep making and believing in what comes next?

It does, and I think it's part of why the work looks the way it does. So much of technology right now assumes that bigger, faster, and more intelligent automatically means better or more meaningful. I'm not sure it does. A lot of what we use every day is designed to keep us scrolling, and very little of it can be opened, understood, or fixed by the people using it. That can make technology feel like something that just happens to us.

Making things that are small, slow, and understandable is my way of responding to that. When you can see how something works, and maybe even build it yourself, you get a little bit of that agency back. I also try not to chase trends. I'm more interested in exploring other ways computing could look and feel, and in leaving room for things that are gentle, strange, or a little bit magical.

What keeps me going is the making itself, and other people. I got here because people generously shared their work with me, so I share mine openly too. Teaching workshops, spending time in community spaces with other makers, and watching someone sew their first circuit and light up when it works reminds me that technology is still something we can shape with our own hands. I also find a lot of joy in small things: a well-made tool, a tiny screen, the feel of a new material in my hands, the satisfying click of a switch. Holding onto that, especially when everything feels uncertain, gives me hope.

Thank you again for the thoughtful questions! Let me know if you need anything else, like images or links. :)
